title: Standard estimators cannot represent fault-tolerant workloads at measured error rates: evaluated, evidence-based uncertainty for quantum resource estimation
abstract: Estimates of the quantum resources needed to run fault-tolerant algorithms are almost always reported as single numbers, even though they rest on uncertain hardware parameters and on cost models that disagree. We present an open, tool-agnostic framework that propagates evidence-based priors over fault-tolerant hardware parameters through five surface-code cost models, adds correlated-input sensitivity analysis, and evaluates the resulting intervals with a pre-registered three-layer protocol. Applied to RSA-2048, ECC-256, AES-256, and a Hubbard-model simulation on a superconducting surface-code architecture, it produces three coupled findings that together undermine the single-number convention. Propagating the error rates hardware has actually demonstrated, whose median across five large-array devices is about 4 x 10^-3 rather than the conventional 10^-3, widens the 90% physical-qubit interval to roughly forty times and lifts its median about 4.6 times above the conventional point estimate. Against the same inputs, five independently structured cost models, including two third-party estimators (the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator and Qualtran) that agree with each other to within about ten percent, disagree by a stable factor of two, a structural uncertainty that no single tool reveals. Most consequentially, both third-party estimators exceed their representable envelope for 80 to 100 percent of the evidence-based parameter space, and the AES-256 gate count overflows one tool's counter outright, so these workloads cannot be represented at measured error rates at all. The optimistic convention conceals every one of these effects. The uncertainty machinery we use is standard. The contribution is its evidence-based application, the pre-registered evaluation, and the finding that standard tools break down precisely where hardware operates.
summary: This paper introduces a robust framework to quantify the uncertainty in quantum resource estimates for fault-tolerant computing. By propagating evidence-based priors through multiple cost models, the authors demonstrate that current single-number estimates are misleading. The results show that using measured hardware error rates drastically increases the required resources and reveals significant structural disagreements between different estimation tools.
main_problem: Standard estimates of quantum resources for fault-tolerant algorithms are reported as single numbers, failing to account for inherent hardware parameter uncertainties and disagreements among cost models.
main_result: Propagating measured error rates significantly widens resource estimates (e.g., 40x wider interval for RSA-2048) compared to optimistic conventions, and structural disagreements between cost models are substantial.
method: The authors developed an open, tool-agnostic framework to propagate evidence-based priors over hardware parameters through multiple surface-code cost models, using advanced sensitivity analysis.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to superconducting two-dimensional nearest-neighbour surface-code architectures, evaluating workloads like RSA-2048, ECC-256, and AES-256.
key_observables: Physical-qubit count, resource intervals (e.g., 90% interval), and the fraction of parameter space an estimator can represent.
important_parameters: Physical two-qubit gate error rate (measured median $\approx 4 \times 10^{-3}$ vs. conventional $10^{-3}$), code distance, and model-specific constants.
main_assumptions: The analysis is limited to the superconducting platform due to available error-rate measurements; the framework relies on propagating priors rather than predicting future performance.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dramatic widening of resource intervals due to measured error rates and the structural disagreement factors between different cost estimation models.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the uncertainty framework, applies it to several cryptographic and simulation workloads on superconducting hardware, and presents three coupled findings that undermine the single-number resource estimation convention.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, uncertainty-aware methodology for estimating resource requirements, which is crucial for any theoretical work aiming to connect abstract quantum algorithms to realistic hardware constraints.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
